n: A new section (chapters 13–23) contains “burdens” — prophecies against foreign nations. It begins with Babylon, which in Isaiah’s day was still under Assyria but would later conquer Judah. In latter-day scripture Babylon also symbolizes the wicked world.

f.g: Hebrew massa’ — a heavy message or oracle, usually of judgment.

n: Raise a signal flag on a bare hill, shout, and wave the troops forward to storm the gates of Babylon’s nobles.

f.g: Wave the hand as a signal.

n: God has summoned His “sanctified ones” — warriors set apart for His purpose — to carry out His judgment. 2 Nephi 23:3 reads “for mine anger is not upon them that rejoice in my highness,” assuring the faithful they are not the target.

f.g: Those consecrated for a task — here, soldiers set apart for holy war.

f.w: even them that rejoice in my highness

n: A roar rises from the mountains — the noise of nations gathering. The Lord of hosts is mustering an army.
They come from far away, from the ends of the earth — the Lord and the weapons of His wrath — to destroy the whole land.
Wail, for the day of the Lord is near, coming as destruction from the Almighty. In Hebrew, “destruction” (shod) and “Almighty” (Shaddai) sound alike.

f.w: the day of the LORD is at hand

n: Everyone’s hands will go limp and every heart melt in fear.
Terror and anguish will grip them like a woman in labor. They will stare at each other in shock, faces burning. 2 Nephi 23:8 omits the comparison to a woman in labor.
The day of the Lord comes with fierce anger to make the land desolate and remove the sinners from it.

f.w: the day of the LORD cometh

n: Stars, sun, and moon will go dark. These cosmic signs describe Babylon’s fall and also the signs before the Second Coming.
God will punish the world for its evil and end the arrogance of the proud and ruthless.
So many will die that people will be rarer than the purest gold of Ophir.

f.g: A distant land famous for fine gold (1 Kings 9:28).

n: The heavens will tremble and the earth shake from its place in the Lord’s fierce anger.
Foreigners in Babylon will scatter like a hunted gazelle or sheep without a shepherd, each fleeing to his own land.
Anyone caught will be killed. 2 Nephi 23:15 reads “Every one that is proud … every one that is joined to the wicked,” focusing judgment on the wicked.
Isaiah describes the horrors of ancient conquest: children killed, houses plundered, women violated. War’s cruelty is the bitter harvest of Babylon’s own violence.
God will stir up the Medes, who cannot be bribed with silver or gold. The Medes and Persians conquered Babylon in 539 BC.

f.g: A people of ancient Iran, allied with Persia under Cyrus.

n: Their archers will be merciless, sparing not even the young.
Babylon — the jewel of kingdoms and pride of the Chaldeans — will be overthrown as completely as Sodom and Gomorrah.

f.g: Chaldeans, the people who ruled Babylon in its last great era.

n: It will never again be inhabited; even nomads and shepherds will avoid it. Babylon declined over centuries and today lies in ruins in Iraq.
Desert animals will live in its ruins — howling creatures, owls, and wild goats dancing among the rubble.

f.g: Wild goats, or goat-demons of folklore.

n: Hyenas and jackals will howl in its palaces. Babylon’s time is near. 2 Nephi 23:22 adds: “For I will destroy her speedily; yea, for I will be merciful unto my people, but the wicked shall perish.”

f.w: her days shall not be prolonged
